st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s separation of AI access from productive performance and materially extends it with randomized legal-education evidence: untrained access did not improve scores, while targeted instruction substantially improved use and performance. It also provides a concrete counterexample to claims that weaker users automatically benefit most, while remaining limited to student examination performance rather than careers or labour-market rewards.
qs: Compared to participants who only had access to an LLM, participants who received the intervention reported substantially higher rates of GenAI usage and achieved, on average, scores that were better by nearly one fine grade.

More broadly, these findings challenge the view that GenAI primarily benefits lower-skilled workers: without training, higher-ability practitioners opt out while lowerability users adopt but unproductively.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s augmentation-and-verification framing and materially strengthens its claim that tool access alone is insufficient. Its randomized experiment isolates targeted training as a complementary input, finding improved adoption and legal-analysis performance with instruction but no average benefit from untrained access, while preserving caveats about external validity and mechanism.
qs: Conversely, access to GenAI without training does not improve performance on average and may be unproductive, although the available evidence does not allow firm conclusions about negative effects.
For legal educators and practitioners, these findings underscore the importance of coordinated investment in both GenAI tools and user training.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s conditional-productivity proposition and materially strengthens it with randomized evidence from legal analysis: brief training increased both GenAI adoption and examination performance, whereas access alone did not improve average performance. It also supports the cluster’s caution that gains depend on complementary knowledge and cannot be inferred from access or usage alone.
qs: Compared to participants who only had access to an LLM, participants who received the intervention reported substantially higher rates of GenAI usage and achieved, on average, scores that were better by nearly one fine grade.
The productivity effects of GenAI are not technologically predetermined but depend on complementary investments in knowledge and capability.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

kp.k: Randomized experiment isolates training alongside optional AI access
kp.d: The study tested HKU LLB and JD contract-law students on 30 November 2025. Of 213 registrants, 164 completed: 49 without AI access, 57 with optional DeepSeek access, and 58 with access plus training. All could use Westlaw. The open-book issue-spotter allowed fifteen minutes for reading and sixty minutes for typing; all participants used the maximum time. Answers were anonymized and shuffled before grading. One participant assigned to training missed the video and was relabelled into the untrained group.
qs: Ultimately, 164 of the 213 participants who signed up finished the study: 49 from Group 1, 57 from Group 2, and 58 from Group 3.
Accordingly, access to an LLM in our experiment was optional rather than required.
All 164 validly submitted answers were anonymized and shuffled before being graded.

kp.k: Brief training teaches assistance rather than unverified reliance
kp.d: The intervention combined a nine-minute, thirty-second video with a five-question quiz. It taught repeated prompting, task decomposition, feedback, and a worked example unrelated to the tested issues. Drawing on professional competence, it instructed students to use AI only where they possessed sufficient knowledge to check outputs, seek ideas rather than delegate solutions, and verify facts, rules, and cases. This is a human-supervised augmentation model, not autonomous legal practice.
qs: They also had to complete a five-question multiple-choice quiz about the contents of the video before starting the examination.
Generic LLMs produce responses based on probabilistic models of language and there is no guarantee that the text they generate make sound or accurate claims.
the user should ask the LLM to give ideas or directions for solving a legal problem rather than relying on it for a solution

kp.k: Training significantly increases self-reported AI adoption
kp.d: DeepSeek use rose from 15 of 57 untrained participants (26.32%) to 24 of 58 trained participants (41.38%), a 15.06-percentage-point difference. The reported p = 0.044 uses a one-tailed z-test; the authors also report p = 0.045 for the t-test prescribed by preregistration. Adoption was measured through a post-examination questionnaire rather than observed interaction records.
qs: Of the 57 participants in Group 2, 15 declared that they used DeepSeek during the examination, giving an adoption rate of 26.32%.
By comparison, 24 of 58 participants in Group 3 declared such use, giving an adoption rate of 41.38%.
The difference of 15.06% points is statistically significant (p = 0.044*, one-tailed z-test).

kp.k: Training improves grades relative to untrained access
kp.d: Mean grade points were 2.290 without AI, 2.251 with untrained access, and 2.521 with trained access. Training improved scores by 0.270 points relative to untrained access, roughly one fine grade (p = 0.027, one-tailed). Its 0.231-point advantage over no AI did not reach conventional significance (p = 0.064, one-tailed). Untrained access's 0.039-point decline was statistically insignificant (p = 0.790, two-tailed), so the study does not establish an overall grade penalty from access alone.
qs: Participants in Group 3 did better than participants in Group 2 on the same measure, indicating that the treatment intervention increased the quality of answers (d = 0.270; p = 0.027*, one-tailed t-test).

Participants in Group 3 also appeared to outscore participants in Group 1 although the improvement does not attain conventional levels of statistical significance (d = 0.231; p = 0.064, one-tailed t-test).

kp.k: Issue coverage and readability show no significant improvements
kp.d: Mean issues missed were 1.102 without AI, 1.228 with untrained access, and 0.983 with trained access; reported comparisons against no AI were insignificant. Mean Flesch–Kincaid grade levels were 12.845, 12.379, and 12.131 respectively, also without significant differences against no AI. The authors suggest possible writing benefits, but these measures do not establish improved issue coverage or readability.
qs: Overall, there is no evidence that access to DeepSeek alone enhanced participants’ performance on the examination as measured by grade point or by number of issues missed.

There are no statistically significant differences in readability between answers in Group 1 and Group 2 (d = -0.466; p = 0.253, two-tailed t-test) or between Group 1 and Group 3 (d = -0.714; p = 0.075, two-tailed t-test).

kp.k: Untrained access produces shorter answers, suggesting interaction costs
kp.d: Average answer lengths were 1059.673 words without AI, 895.737 with untrained access, and 1001.638 with training. Untrained answers were significantly shorter than both comparison groups (p = 0.019 and p = 0.042, two-tailed), but these tests were not preregistered. The authors propose unfruitful AI interaction consuming writing time as a possible explanation, not a measured mechanism.
qs: Answers in Group 2 are significantly shorter than those in Groups 1 and 3 (p = 0.019* and p = 0.042*, respectively, two-tailed t-tests; tests not pre-registered).
One possible explanation for our data is that Group 2 participants who had access to DeepSeek without receiving the training intervention spent time interacting unfruitfully with the LLM.

kp.k: Training reduces rule errors but not case misstatements
kp.d: Rule misstatements, which include omitted rules, averaged 2.469 without AI, 2.579 with untrained access, and 2.155 with training. Training reduced this measure relative to untrained access by 0.424 (p = 0.014, one-tailed). Case misstatements meant existing cases irrelevant to or unsupported by the argument: averages were 0.020, 0.193, and 0.207. Untrained access increased case misstatements against no AI (p = 0.017, one-tailed), while training did not significantly improve them. No fabricated cases appeared in any answer; this is distinct from correct use of real authorities.
qs: The Rule Misstatements variable was calculated by counting instances of rule omissions or misstatements across these four issues.
We recorded zero Case Hallucination for all the 164 answers.

Group 2 recorded a significantly higher number of Rule Misstatements compared with Group 3 (d = -0.424; p = 0.014*, one-tailed t-test), which suggests training can effectively help participants to state rule more accurately.
Group 2 recorded a significantly higher number of Case Misstatements compared with Group 1 (d = 0.173; p = 0.017*, one-tailed t-test).

kp.k: Framework separates adoption from effectiveness of AI use
kp.d: The theoretical model treats AI's net contribution as capability gains offset by expected error losses and adoption costs. Complex tasks have higher error probabilities and costs; training is assumed not to reduce effectiveness or increase adoption costs. It may improve existing users' performance or induce previously reluctant users to adopt by reducing costs and perceived risks. These are modelling assumptions and proposed mechanisms, not independently measured effects.
qs: We begin by sketching a simple conceptual framework in which GenAI can enhance human productivity through two distinct channels: by expanding the scope of GenAI use—that is, the set of tasks for which users are willing to adopt the technology— and by improving the effectiveness of use conditional on adoption.
For induced users, training operates through the extensive margin by lowering adoption costs or mitigating perceived risks, thereby expanding the set of tasks for which GenAI use becomes attractive.

kp.k: Adoption mechanism remains suggestive and assumption-dependent
kp.d: Principal stratification partially identifies effects because training may affect both adoption and existing users' effectiveness, violating the standard instrumental-variable exclusion restriction. Under monotonicity, no training effect for never-users, and grade support restrictions, bounds do not establish either effect's sign. Adding strict mean dominance produces an adoption lower bound of 1.059 and effectiveness upper bound of 0.419. Their ordering reverses beyond a dominance relaxation of 0.640; wide, overlapping bootstrap confidence intervals prevent a firm conclusion that adoption dominates.
qs: The bounds are wide and uninformative about the sign of either effect.
This assumption states that trained induced users perform as well as trained always users up to a tolerance 𝛾.

Confidence intervals are wide and overlapping, so we cannot statistically reject effectiveness as the dominant mechanism, but the point estimate ordering holds unless always users outperform induced users posttraining by more than this margin.

kp.k: Ability-related adoption patterns are descriptive, not causal
kp.d: The authors challenge the narrative that AI primarily benefits lower-skilled workers, proposing that higher-ability users require training before adopting while lower-ability users may adopt unproductively. Top examination-grade-quartile adoption was 0.0% (0/6) without training versus 41.7% (5/12) with training. However, ability was proxied by the same post-treatment examination outcome, quartile cells were small, and this analysis was not preregistered. It therefore does not confirm differential effects by pre-existing ability.
qs: because grade point is itself a post-treatment outcome from the same examination, it cannot serve as a clean pre-treatment measure of ability.
The quartile classification is therefore potentially endogenous to the treatment, and the pattern  in Table 4 should be interpreted as descriptive rather than confirmatory.
Our use of exam GPA as a post-hoc proxy for ability is suggestive but imperfect: the quartile cell sizes are small and the analysis was not pre-registered.

kp.k: Professional adoption gap motivates task-specific human training
kp.d: As background rather than original findings, the paper contrasts controlled studies reporting legal-work efficiency gains with surveys reporting limited adoption and confidence. It cites a 2025 survey of more than 2,800 lawyers reporting GenAI use by 21% of firms, and LexisNexis's finding that 74% of firms identified fabricated content as a major barrier. The authors frame judgment-intensive, error-sensitive legal analysis as a boundary application where model capability alone does not ensure productive human use.
qs: A 2025 survey of more than 2,800 lawyers reports that only 21% of law firms currently use GenAI tools (American Bar Association 2025).
Notably, in one survey, 74% of firms identify concerns about hallucinated or fabricated content as a major barrier to deployment (LexisNexis 2024).
Effective human-AI collaboration, in such settings, cannot be assumed — it may need to be taught.

kp.k: Educators and employers should jointly invest in training
kp.d: The authors recommend integrating human–AI collaboration into professional education, combining prompting and interrogation skills with understanding of model limitations. For law firms and corporate legal departments, they advocate coordinated investment in access and human capital. They predict that organization- and occupation-specific training may slow diffusion and temporarily advantage successful early adopters; these organizational implications extend beyond the experiment's measured individual outcomes.
qs: In educational settings, they support proposals to incorporate instruction  on effective human–AI collaboration as a core component of professional training.
For law firms and legal departments, the findings suggest that successful GenAI integration requires coordinated investment in both technology access and human capital.
Such customization may slow diffusion and generate temporary advantages for early adopters who successfully integrate GenAI into their workflows.

kp.k: Findings do not establish durable practice-wide productivity gains
kp.d: The authors limit generalization from a single institution's students, one timed examination, one tool, and a brief intervention. Real legal work is collaborative, iterative, and organizationally embedded. The study does not establish persistence, effects across experience levels or practice areas, or how organizational incentives influence training. They call for longitudinal and field studies, independent pre-treatment ability measures, and investigation of training timing, intensity, content, and changing model capabilities.
qs: While such examinations assess individual legal reasoning under time constraints, legal work in practice is often collaborative, iterative, and embedded in organizational processes.
Although examination scores provide a meaningful and widely used proxy for legal competence, they do not reveal whether the benefits of training persist or evolve with repeated use.
Finally, our analysis focuses on individual-level performance and abstracts from organizational and institutional factors that shape technology adoption in professional settings.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Chen and Bao claim that brief, task-specific training increases voluntary GenAI adoption and improves legal-analysis quality compared with providing access alone.
pts.d: In their law-student experiment, training increased self-reported DeepSeek use from 26.32% to 41.38% and raised mean examination grade points from 2.251 to 2.521. Rule omissions or misstatements declined from 2.579 to 2.155. The authors frame these as improvements in human–AI collaboration, not replacement of legal judgment. The trained group also outscored the no-AI group, but that comparison did not reach conventional statistical significance. Although the conclusion refers to more comprehensive issue spotting, the results report no statistically significant differences in missed issues.

pts.k: The authors claim that access without instruction produces no demonstrated average performance benefit and may undermine short-run productivity.
pts.d: Untrained access was associated with a small, statistically insignificant grade-point decline relative to no AI, significantly shorter answers, and significantly more cases cited in support of arguments they did not support. Training improved rule statements but did not significantly reduce case misstatements relative to untrained access. No nonexistent cases were cited in any group. The authors suggest that unproductive interaction with the model may consume time otherwise available for writing, consulting authorities, and verification; this is a proposed explanation rather than a directly measured mechanism.

pts.k: Training may improve aggregate performance primarily by inducing additional users to adopt, rather than by improving the effectiveness of people who would use AI anyway.
pts.d: Chen and Bao distinguish adoption by induced users from effectiveness improvements among always users. Their principal-stratification point estimates favor adoption as the larger mechanism under an additional mean-dominance assumption, but they explicitly do not claim definitive identification. Without that assumption, estimated bounds allow either positive or negative effects for both mechanisms.

pts.k: The authors challenge the generalization that GenAI primarily benefits lower-skilled workers, proposing that training can unlock adoption among higher-ability professionals.
pts.d: Their interpretation is that less-skilled users may adopt without instruction but use the technology ineffectively, while more-skilled users may initially opt out because of perceived risks. Training may change this selection pattern. They describe adoption in the highest examination-grade quartile increasing from 0 of 6 untrained participants to 5 of 12 trained participants. They qualify this as descriptive, not confirmatory, because ability was proxied by the same post-treatment examination outcome, subgroup samples were small, and the analysis was not preregistered.

pts.k: The source frames near-term legal AI as augmentation and predicts that complementary training investment will shape uneven organizational adoption and productivity gains.
pts.d: Chen and Bao argue that legal educators should teach practical interaction skills, understanding of model limitations, and human verification. They recommend coordinated investment in tools and human capital by law firms and corporate legal departments. They further propose that task-specific training requirements could slow diffusion, that unsuccessful untrained use could foster resistance, and that organizations integrating AI successfully could enjoy temporary early-adopter advantages. These organizational and market implications are extrapolations from the experiment, not measured firm-level outcomes; no dates, employment-loss estimates, or revenue forecasts are supplied.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a three-condition experiment measuring immediate examination output and self-reported AI adoption.
pts.d: The experiment took place on 30 November 2025 among University of Hong Kong LLB and JD contract-law students. Of 213 registered participants randomly assigned, 164 completed: 49 without AI access, 57 with optional DeepSeek access alone, and 58 with access plus a 9-minute-30-second video and five-question quiz. All groups could use Westlaw and course materials. Answers were anonymized and shuffled before rubric-based grading. One participant assigned to training missed the video and was relabelled as untrained. Adoption increased by 15.06 percentage points (p = 0.044, one-tailed z-test); trained-versus-untrained grades increased by 0.270 points (p = 0.027, one-tailed t-test); rule errors or omissions declined by 0.424 (p = 0.014, one-tailed t-test). Trained-versus-no-AI grades differed by 0.231 (p = 0.064, one-tailed). Untrained-versus-no-AI grades differed by -0.039 (p = 0.790, two-tailed). Untrained answers were approximately 164 words shorter than no-AI answers (p = 0.019, non-preregistered two-tailed test), and case misstatements increased by 0.173 (p = 0.017, one-tailed). Everyone used the full allotted time, so the experiment measures work quality under a fixed time constraint rather than observed completion-time savings.

pts.k: Mechanism and skill-distribution claims rely on assumption-dependent analysis and descriptive subgroups, rather than separately randomized mechanisms or independent ability measurements.
pts.d: The principal-stratification analysis assumes training does not discourage adoption, has no effect on never users, and outcomes remain within the grade-point support of 1.0–4.3. Under support restrictions alone, adoption bounds are -0.454 to 2.846 and effectiveness bounds are -1.093 to 1.226. Adding strict mean dominance yields an adoption lower bound of 1.059 and effectiveness upper bound of 0.419. The 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for those endpoints are respectively -0.364 to 1.740 and -0.049 to 0.938. The higher-ability adoption interpretation draws on post-treatment grade quartiles, not baseline ability data. Organizational diffusion and early-adopter claims are theoretical implications rather than results from organizational or labor-market observation.

pts.k: The authors contextualize their findings with earlier legal-task experiments, adoption surveys, and evidence of AI-generated legal errors; these are cited findings, not their own measurements.
pts.d: The paper attributes greater-than-50% improvements in time-adjusted work quality using RAG and reasoning models to Schwarcz et al. (2025), up-to-30% time reductions with AI highlighting to Nielsen et al. (2024), and 10–30% time savings on basic legal tasks to Choi et al. (2024). It contrasts these with a 2025 survey of over 2,800 lawyers reporting GenAI use by 21% of firms and a LexisNexis survey reporting fabricated-content concerns at 74% of firms. It cites Dahl et al. (2024) for hallucination rates as high as 58% on certain legal tasks and Charlotin's database, accessed 28 January 2026, for at least 851 court opinions addressing AI-fabricated submissions. Those task error rates and court incidents are distinct from this experiment's zero nonexistent-case citations. Chien and Kim's legal-aid field study supplies supportive but self-reported evidence about concierge assistance, productivity, and adoption intentions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The demonstrated effects are immediate and specific to optional DeepSeek use in one timed contract-law examination; durability and generalizability remain open.
pts.d: The November 2025 intervention was assessed in a single 75-minute examination, comprising 15 minutes of reading and 60 minutes of typing, reported in the 2026 paper. Training addressed legal issue spotting, prompting, feedback, and checking facts, rules, and authorities, rather than generic AI literacy. The source conditions productive use on sufficient user knowledge to verify output and on treating the model as assistance rather than an authoritative solution. The authors caution that professional practice is more collaborative and iterative, other experience levels and practice areas may differ, and repeated-use or long-term training effects were not measured. Predictions about short-run productivity, longer-run innovation, and temporary competitive advantages have no quantified horizon.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied population is law students; the proposed implications concern legal educators, practicing lawyers, law firms, and in-house legal departments.
pts.d: Students receive potential gains in adoption and assessed legal-analysis quality from instruction. Legal educators are urged to incorporate human–AI collaboration into professional training. Practicing lawyers are envisaged as continuing to exercise judgment and verify AI output, with training potentially altering adoption differently across ability levels. Provider-side law firms and buyer-side corporate legal departments are urged to invest jointly in tools and staff capabilities; organizations that tailor training effectively may gain temporary advantages. The paper does not directly estimate effects on clients, access to justice, fees, staffing structures, employment, or legal-market shares. Its legal-aid discussion is supporting literature, not a demonstrated public-access outcome of this experiment.
